$comment: The banned-register list for spec prose, held as data so the list grows without touching a script. Companion to docs/style/spec-language-guide.md, which is the human-readable form of the same rules; the guide explains, this file is what a program reads. srs#569 consumes it to build scripts/check-spec-language.mjs, together with its own allowlist of grandfathered sites. Two lists: `patterns` are regex-shaped and apply per prose field; `rules` are everything else, each declaring whether a program or a reviewer enforces it. Nothing here is a check on its own — this file has no runner and needs no entry in scripts/checks.json.

normativeSites.$comment: Where RFC 2119 keywords are legitimate, and where the `normative` scope below applies. No exposition_role field exists or will (srs#556 ruling, 2026-09-05): a leaf's Type is its role. `types` names the typeNamespace/typeName pairs whose records may carry RFC 2119 keywords outside a normative_statement field — `invariant` and `mechanism` (RFC-042 Change G, landed via srs#562).

patterns.pattern: \b(?:in today's|in the (?:modern|current) (?:landscape|world|era)|a testament to|plays? an? (?:key|major|central|important) role|unlock(?:s|ing)? the (?:power|potential))\b
patterns.substitution: Delete. A specification has no audience to persuade.
Name the actor: the validator, the loader, the renderer, the CLI, an implementation.
The keyword carries the force. Drop the adverb, or drop the keyword and describe.
RFC 2119 keywords are uppercase in a normative statement, so a reader can find them by grep.

rules.statement: A prose field carries at most 400 words. Above that, split into child records, or move the worked example into a typed `example` record.
At most one em-dash per paragraph, and none inside a normative statement. A cap, not a ban: the em-dash is house voice, and the cap removes only the machine-gun rhythm that reads as generated.

RFC 2119 keywords appear only in a normative_statement field, or in a record whose Type is named in normativeSites.types (invariant today; mechanism once RFC-042 lands). Explanatory prose never uses them.
The first sentence of a prose field does not restate the record's title. Comparable mechanically: strip stopwords from both and measure the overlap.
Not every bullet in a list opens with a bold lead-in and a colon. Countable: bullets matching `^[-*] \*\*...\*\*:` against total bullets in the field.

A constraint states the rule and nothing else. Its reason belongs in a design-note record linked by `explains`. A reviewer can see a `because` clause that a regex cannot separate from a legitimate conditional.
A term is defined once, as a `concept` record (srs#561), and never redefined in prose. Mechanical once concept records exist and cover the vocabulary; review-only until then.
A bulleted list carries genuinely parallel items. Two sentences of prose beaten into three bullets is a judgement call, not a pattern.
Sections vary in length because subjects vary in size. Suspicious uniformity is visible across a part, not inside one field.
Lists are as long as the subject requires. A third item added for cadence is only detectable by reading it.
A MUST marks a requirement an implementation can fail. A description of behaviour is written as a description. The corpus runs 92% mandatory, so each new MUST earns its keyword.
Where a worked example settles the question, write the example instead of the paragraph, as a typed `example` record.
